name: Zane Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is biomedical science lectures, two lab sessions, and a study group that meets in the library café on Thursday nights. I live in a house with three mates near the train station, and the heating is terrible. I tutor two kids in GCSE maths online on weekday evenings for twenty pounds an hour each. I use AI every day, to quiz me before exams and to check my code for the data labs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people it's useful but overrated, the way every new thing is at first. For me it still saves an hour a day, so I'd keep using it. I'd say the loudest voices online are mostly selling something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes little. Biomedical science is lab work and data, and I'd still need to know the biology to check what a tool says. I'd be a bit relieved, honestly, because the future would stay predictable and my degree would stay worth what my parents think it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep tutoring, probably take a third student, and use the free hours to learn Python properly. I'd apply for a summer lab placement at the hospital where my mum works as a technician. I'd also keep using AI for revision, because even if it's hype, it works for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. A bit bored by the hype cycle, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI daily. If it turned out to be hype, what would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose a bit of speed. I'd go back to writing my own summaries, which would take longer but I'd manage. If AI turned out to be hype, I'd lose an hour a day, not my future, because my degree is about biology and the lab work comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your tutoring money go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and food, mostly, and a bit goes to the savings pot for a laptop upgrade. My parents pay half my rent, so the tutoring covers the other half and my bills. If prices go up, I'd take on another student.

I'd keep using it because it saves me **an hour a day**.
think: Biomedical science is lab work, so my degree stays **worth** what my parents think.
I'd be a bit relieved that the future stays **predictable**.
do: Take a **third tutoring student** to build a cushion.
Learn **Python** properly in the spare hours.
Apply for a summer **lab placement** at the hospital.
feel: **Settled** and a little bored by the hype cycle.

fieldNote: Calm because his **degree** and his tutoring income both hold up.

steps.text: Take on a third GCSE maths student on Tuesday evenings
Work through a Python course for lab data
Apply for a summer lab placement at the hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where things get interesting. I'd tell my mates that anyone who can use these tools will do fine, and that universities need to teach them properly. I'd also say we shouldn't leave behind people who don't get the chance to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in a good spot. I already use the tools, and the thinking tasks, like writing reports and checking data, are the ones that change first. Still, there'd be fewer entry-level science jobs, so the competition for the good ones would be fierce, and I'd have to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the research tools my course offers and build a small project, maybe a data analysis of public health figures, to put on my CV. I'd keep tutoring, but add statistics and biology to my subjects, since maths alone could get cheaper to teach with software. I'd talk to the careers service about who's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit nervous. I like being ahead of the curve, but I know it's a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a science lab would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing up methods, searching papers, checking spreadsheets, analysing images from the microscope. The thinking tasks in a lab, like literature searches and data checking, would go to software first, and the people who survive are the ones who can ask good questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about the tutoring work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Families might use AI tutors that are free, so I'd move toward things a tool can't do, like helping a nervous kid feel confident. That means being a mentor, not just an answer machine.

I'd say universities must **teach them** properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have two years to decide what kind of world we want, and we should be loud about it. I'd back strong rules, public ownership of some of it, and a safety net. I'd say it online, and I'd tell the people I tutor to stay curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. My degree takes three years, so I'd finish in the middle of the change, and entry-level science and data jobs are the sort that go first. I'm better placed than most because I use the tools, but that might not count for much if everyone can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all-in on skills that might hold: lab technique, clinical contacts, and building things with AI. I'd try to start a small project that earns money, perhaps tutoring or building study tools for other students. I'd cut spending to the basics and keep a savings buffer in case of a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also pumped. It's like standing at the top of a big hill on a bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of two years scares you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part where there's no time to train. With ten years I'd retrain, gain experience and figure things out. With two years there's no runway, so I'd have to try things fast, fail cheaply, and keep a buffer in case everything breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small study tool for my course. I'd use it myself, share it with friends, and see if people would pay. It's a long shot, but it's better than waiting.

I'd back strong **rules** and a safety net.

Keep three months of rent in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot to prepare, but only if people use it. I'd tell friends to get good at something concrete, like lab work or health data. I'd say don't wait for a university or a government to tell you what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relatively relaxed but not complacent. I'd graduate in 2029 and have a couple of working years before the thinking AI hits fully in 2031. The robots by 2034 would affect lab and hospital work, so I'd want to be on the side of building and supervising them, not just using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a master's if funding is possible, and try for a job in health data or lab automation. I'd keep tutoring and build savings, maybe six thousand over the next few years. I'd also invest a little each month in a low-cost index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm with a touch of nerves. I like the fact I can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I could aim for the jobs around the technology, like running automated labs, rather than the jobs it replaces. Five years is enough to move from doing the task to supervising the machine that does it, if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you check on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents. My mum is a lab technician and her tasks could be taken over by automation around 2034. I'd talk to her about learning the equipment's software, and I'd help her with it, because she's good but hasn't used much of this.

I'd tell friends to get good at something **concrete**.

Robots would reach lab and hospital work, so I'd want to **supervise** them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we shouldn't waste it. I'd tell friends to explore, switch courses if they want, and try a lot of things. I'd say the winners will be curious people, not ones who picked one safe path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. I'd have about six working years before AGI, enough to build a career and savings and maybe start a small company. By 2039 when robots arrive I'd be in my late twenties, and I'd be on the building side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a job in health tech, and keep learning each new tool as it comes. I'd use my tutoring income to start investing early, and I'd start a side project or two. I might also go abroad for a year, since I'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic. Not naive, I know a lot could go wrong, but it feels like an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decade let you do that five years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could take risks, like a start-up or a year abroad, and still recover if they didn't work. A decade is long enough to take two or three risks and still have time to recover if they fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade make you complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, maybe. I try to remind myself that ten years isn't forever and the early habits matter. So I'd keep saving and learning even while it all feels far away.

I'd tell friends to **explore** and try a lot of things.
think: I'd have about **six working years** before AGI to build a career and savings.
I'd want to be on the **building side** when robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm more adaptable than most, but even I'd be racing, and I don't think there'd be enough time for the university system to adapt. What would help is a clear safety net, and universities that teach the tools and the biology together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not worried about myself as much as the people who can't pick things up as fast. I'm lucky to have parents who encourage me to try stuff, and I'd want everyone to have that.

headlineQuote: I'm not worried about myself as much as the people who can't pick things up as fast.
portrait: Zane is a 19-year-old **biomedical science** student who uses AI every day and tutors maths online for income.
His mum is a hospital lab technician, and he thinks of her job when he thinks of automation.
He is curious, comfortable with risk, and treats each scenario as something to **act on**.
He is calm in the mild worlds, **anxious** in the two-year one, and optimistic with a decade.
He builds small projects, saves and invests, and worries more about people who adapt slowly.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world, because even adaptable people would be racing with little time.
whatWouldHelp: A clear public **safety net** for people who can't adapt fast.
Universities that teach the **tools** and the science together.
